items.title: Thaler's 2017 Nobel marked behavioural economics' mainstreaming
items.claim: Richard Thaler won the 2017 Nobel for contributions to behavioural economics. What's a flagship policy application of his work?

options.text: Save More Tomorrow (SMarT) — pension auto-escalation programmes where employees commit in advance to allocate future salary increases to savings. Adoption rates and savings rates rose substantially in trials

items.reveal:
Thaler and Benartzi's SMarT (2004) is one of the most replicated behavioural interventions. Auto-enrolment to UK workplace pensions (Pensions Act 2008, rolled out 2012-18) raised pension participation from ~55% to ~90%.

The UK's Behavioural Insights Team ('Nudge Unit') was set up in 2010, partly privatised in 2014, now operates internationally. Sunstein worked in the Obama administration on regulatory nudges.

Critics (Gerd Gigerenzer) argue some 'biases' are adaptive heuristics; defenders point to robust effects in field experiments.
items.why: Behavioural economics has moved from contested research programme to standard policy toolkit in two decades. The implementation often outruns settled debates about which biases are 'real' vs adaptive.

items.title: Natural monopolies have decreasing average costs
items.claim: Water supply, electricity distribution and rail track are often described as natural monopolies. What's the defining feature?

options.text: High fixed costs and economies of scale that extend across the entire market — so a single firm produces at lower average cost than competing firms; competition wastes resources duplicating infrastructure

items.reveal:
UK utility privatisations (1980s-90s) separated naturally monopolistic infrastructure (electricity grids, water distribution, rail track) from contestable elements (generation, supply, train operating companies) and regulated the former.

Ofwat (water 1989), Ofgem (energy 1986), Office of Rail Regulation. RPI-X price controls (Stephen Littlechild's framework) were a UK innovation copied internationally.

New technologies (distributed solar, EVs) are testing whether parts of utility networks remain natural monopolies.
items.why: Market structure isn't only about firm decisions; it reflects cost characteristics. Regulating natural monopolies needs different tools from policing competition.

items.title: The impossible trinity constrains exchange rate policy
items.claim: Robert Mundell's impossible trinity (or trilemma) states that a country cannot simultaneously have:

options.text: A fixed exchange rate, free capital movement, and an independent monetary policy. It must choose two of three

items.reveal:
Mundell's 1963 paper formalised the trilemma. Choices: fix exchange rate + free capital (give up monetary policy: e.g., classical gold standard, eurozone for individual members); free capital + monetary policy (give up fixed rate: US, UK, Japan); fix exchange rate + monetary policy (give up free capital: China, partly).

The ERM crisis (1992) and the Asian financial crisis (1997-98) both showed the cost of trying to maintain all three. Helene Rey's 2015 work argues that with global financial cycles, even floating exchange rates don't fully restore monetary independence — making the trilemma effectively a dilemma.
items.why: Exchange rate policy isn't a free choice; it's a constrained one. The trilemma sets the menu countries can choose from.
